planting.note: Set out container-grown plants well after all danger of cold has passed into warm, humid, sheltered shade.

directions: Phenakospermum guyannense is a giant, non-woody herb native to the understory of lowland Amazonian rainforest across the Guianas, Venezuela, and northern Brazil, where it forms a banana-like clump of paddle-shaped leaves on short pseudostems reaching well over fifteen feet tall. It produces a branched inflorescence of waxy cream to pale yellow flowers followed by blue-coated seeds, placing it in the same family as Strelitzia and Ravenala despite its superficial resemblance to a banana or traveler's palm. In cultivation it needs constant warmth, high humidity, and shelter from direct midday sun to mimic its native shaded forest-floor habitat, along with rich, constantly moist soil. Owing to its enormous eventual size, it is grown mainly in tropical botanical collections and by specialist exotic-plant growers rather than in typical home gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in filtered light once frost risk has passed.

directions: Pitcairnia corallina is a terrestrial bromeliad native to montane and premontane forest in Peru and Ecuador, distinguished from the familiar rosette-forming tank bromeliads by its soft, grass-like, deciduous leaves that die back during dry periods. Its arching flower scapes carry tubular, coral-red blossoms pollinated by hummingbirds in the wild, a trait shared with many of its several hundred Pitcairnia relatives found from Mexico to Argentina. Unlike epiphytic bromeliads, it grows rooted in leaf litter or rocky soil on shaded slopes and stream banks, so it prefers filtered light, humus-rich well-drained soil, and regular moisture during active growth with a drier rest when the leaves senesce. It is grown by specialist bromeliad collectors who prize the genus for its flower color rather than for the architectural rosettes typical of other bromeliads.

planting.note: Transplant into a coarse, moisture-retentive, free-draining mix in bright shade once nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Cochliostema odoratissimum is a large, clump-forming perennial in the dayflower family native to humid lowland and premontane forests of Costa Rica, Panama, and northern South America, where it grows as an epiphyte in leaf-litter pockets or terrestrially on shaded banks. Its wide, strap-shaped leaves form a basal rosette from which arise striking blue to violet flowers with curled, spiraling petal-like structures and a strong, sweet fragrance that gives the species its name. Because it comes from the deeply shaded forest floor and canopy crotches, it needs bright shade, high humidity, and a coarse, free-draining, moisture-retentive mix rather than direct sun or standard potting soil. It is propagated and grown by specialist tropical and epiphyte collectors for its unusual flower form and scent rather than offered in general nursery trade.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into lean, fast-draining soil in full coastal sun.

directions: Ochagavia carnea is a terrestrial bromeliad endemic to coastal bluffs and rocky slopes near Valparaiso in central Chile, where it forms dense rosettes of stiff, spine-tipped silvery-green leaves adapted to salt spray, wind, and intense coastal sun. Its compact flower heads nestle low in the rosette center and open in shades of salmon to flesh-pink, the feature behind both its species epithet and its common name. Thriving in lean, fast-draining soil with little supplemental water once established, it tolerates drought, wind, and the brief cool spells typical of its Pacific coastal habitat far better than tropical rainforest bromeliads. It remains a specialist plant grown mainly by succulent and bromeliad collectors drawn to its toughness and architectural rosette form.
